title: The IBM 350 hard drive
hook: The first hard drive weighed about a tonne and held less than one song's worth of data.
peek: In 1956 IBM shipped the first computer with a hard disk drive. Its 50 spinning platters filled a cabinet the size of two refrigerators, and the whole thing stored about 5 million characters, roughly one modern MP3.
lede: In 1956 IBM introduced the 305 RAMAC computer, and with it the IBM 350, the first commercial hard disk drive. It stacked 50 metal platters, each 24 inches across, in a cabinet that weighed about a tonne. All of that stored 5 million characters. Because each character used 6 bits, that is about 3.75 megabytes in today's terms.

bullets.text: RAMAC stood for Random Access Method of Accounting and Control. Before it, business records lived on tape or punched cards and had to be read in order. A disk let the machine jump straight to any record, such as one customer's account.
A single access arm moved up and down the stack to reach the right platter, then slid in to the right track. Finding a record took most of a second, which felt quick next to rewinding a reel of tape.
Customers usually leased rather than bought. IBM charged about $3,200 a month for the RAMAC system, so each megabyte of storage cost far more per month than a whole modern hard drive.
Shipping a drive meant heavy lifting. A well-known IBM photo shows a RAMAC unit being loaded into an aircraft's cargo hold with a forklift, a reminder of how physical data storage once was.
